deep.reconstruction:
There is no mathematics on this page: no formulas, computations or derivations. It is the opening of section V of Riemann's physiological essay on the mechanics of the middle ear. That essay was published posthumously by Henle in 1867 as 'Mechanik des Ohres' and is reprinted in Riemann's Gesammelte Werke.

Content in modern terms:
(1) Earlier sections set out the probable geometric conditions on the position of the ossicles (malleus, incus, stapes). These conditions keep the ossicles fitting closely together at the joints at all times, without producing noticeably non-uniform tension either in the rim of the oval-window (vestibular) membrane or in the tympanic membrane.
(2) Section V now asks by what means the ossicles are given, and kept in, this correct position.
(3) The parenthetical answer is qualitative: mostly by mutually opposing forces. These balance each other in the correct position. If the ossicle were displaced, they would drive it back. In modern language the correct configuration is a stable equilibrium, with a restoring force or positive-definite stiffness about it. Riemann does not formalise this.
(4) The candidate sources of these forces are listed: the two muscles regulating the ossicles (tensor tympani and stapedius), the joint capsules, the ligaments, the mucosal folds, and the two membranes the ossicles are attached to (tympanic membrane and oval-window annular membrane).
(5) The sentence continues onto the next page. There he notes that several mechanisms could produce the same effect. Choosing among them would need anatomical data on ligament elasticity and tension, which he cannot obtain himself. Alternatively, false hypotheses could be excluded by deriving their improbable consequences.

The page serves the essay's overall aim: a mechanical theory of how the middle ear transmits sound faithfully and adapts during attentive listening.
errors: No mathematical errors, since there is no mathematics. The argument is a qualitative statement of stable equilibrium under opposing elastic and muscular forces, which is physically sound.

results.what: The correct position of the ossicles is maintained by antagonistic forces from muscles, ligaments, capsules, mucosal folds and membranes, balanced in the correct position and restoring it after displacement.
results.modern_name: Stable static equilibrium / restoring forces in middle-ear suspension (ossicular chain mechanics)
results.usually_credited_to: General 19th-century physiology of the middle ear (Helmholtz 1868, 'Die Mechanik der Gehörknöchelchen und des Trommelfells'; earlier anatomical work). Riemann's own posthumous 'Mechanik des Ohres' (1867) contains this text.

deep.surprise_reason: This is a draft page of Riemann's known and published (1867, Henle; Gesammelte Werke) essay 'Mechanik des Ohres'. Its content is purely qualitative physiological reasoning about stable equilibrium of the ossicles, with no new mathematics.
transcription_corrections: Line 8: 'im Rande der Trommelmembran' should read 'im Rande der Vorhofsmembran'. The image shows 'Vorhofsmembran' (the oval-window/stapes membrane). 'Trommelmembran' would also duplicate 'Paukenfell' (the tympanic membrane) in the same sentence.
'aus ihr entfernt würde': the manuscript shows 'ihre' with the final letter cancelled or overwritten, i.e. corrected to 'ihr'.
'zurücktreiben würden': the last word is partially overwritten or struck at the end, with the closing parenthesis attached.
'Gehörknöchelchen' before 'verwachsen sind' carries an interlinear correction of its ending in the manuscript.
Folio marker '14)' at the top left is correct.
